The Age of Exploration. From roughly fourteen hundred to sixteen hundred, this era of European maritime expansion fundamentally transformed the world. Driven by the search for trade routes to Asia, the desire for wealth and spices, missionary zeal, and royal patronage, explorers from Portugal, Spain, England, and France ventured into unknown oceans, mapping coasts and establishing trading posts and colonies. They initiated the transformation of the world into a global system of commerce and conquest.

Prince Henry the Navigator, a Portuguese prince living from thirteen ninety-four to fourteen sixty, sponsored a school of navigation and systematic expeditions along the African coast, establishing trading posts and seeking a sea route to Asia. Vasco da Gama reached India by sea between fourteen ninety-seven and fourteen ninety-eight, rounding Africa's Cape of Good Hope and proving that a direct maritime route to Asia existed. Portugal established a far-flung maritime empire across the Indian Ocean, controlling trade in spices, textiles, and luxuries from East Africa to India to the Indonesian archipelago.

Christopher Columbus sailed for Spain and crossed the Atlantic in fourteen ninety-two seeking a westward route to Asia, but instead reached the Caribbean islands and encountered indigenous peoples, initiating Spanish colonial conquest of the Americas. Spain rapidly conquered vast territories including the Aztec Empire under Hernán Cortés between fifteen nineteen and fifteen twenty-one, and the Inca Empire under Francisco Pizarro between fifteen thirty-two and fifteen seventy-two, plundering gold and silver and establishing a vast colonial enterprise. The Spanish established an empire stretching from Mexico and Central America to South America and the Caribbean.

Ferdinand Magellan, sailing for Spain, led the first expedition to circumnavigate the globe between fifteen nineteen and fifteen twenty-two, proving the world's size and the existence of vast ocean expanses, though Magellan died in the Philippines and his crew completed the voyage. English and French explorers like John Cabot, Jacques Cartier, and Henry Hudson sought alternative routes and established footholds in North America, eventually leading to English and French colonial empires. The Columbian Exchange began with the movement of crops, animals, diseases, technologies, and peoples between Europe and the Americas, with catastrophic consequences for indigenous Americans as disease killed an estimated ninety percent of the population.

Advances in navigation technology including the astrolabe, the magnetic compass, and improved cartography made long ocean voyages feasible, while the caravel, a fast ship design, enabled Portuguese and Spanish exploration. The establishment of trading posts, factories as fortified compounds, and eventually colonies created a framework for sustained European presence and dominance. The Treaty of Tordesillas in fourteen ninety-four divided the non-European world between Spain and Portugal, establishing the principle of European partition of the globe.
